parashot.theme: Gratitude to G-d must be kept not only in hardship but also in plenty.
daily: The name of the parashah, Eikev, can be understood as “heel”: Rashi teaches that one should not neglect even those mitzvot that seem small and are “trampled underfoot.”
“Man does not live by bread alone” (8:3). The manna taught the people that sustenance comes from the Almighty. A person needs spiritual food as well.
“You shall eat, and be satisfied, and bless” (8:10) — the source of the blessing after the meal, Birkat HaMazon. After a meal, try at least briefly giving thanks.
Moshe honestly reminds the people of their mistakes. The Torah does not idealize its heroes: admitting a mistake is the beginning of correction.
After the broken tablets, G-d gave the second ones. The Sages say that both the whole and the broken tablets were kept in the Ark: the past is not erased, but it does not prevent a fresh start.
“You shall love the stranger (the ger), for you were strangers in the land of Egypt” (10:19). The Torah directly commands love for one who has joined the people of Israel.
The second passage of the Shema (11:13–21) speaks of love for G-d and of the connection between our actions and their consequences. It is read daily together with the first.

parashot.summary: Moshe sets before the people a choice between blessing and curse. He commands that sacrifices be brought only in the place that the Almighty will choose, and warns against false prophets and idolatry. The parashah lists the signs of kosher animals, fish and birds, the laws of tithes, debt release in the seventh year and help for the poor. It ends with the laws of the three pilgrimage festivals.
parashot.theme: Freedom of choice: a person chooses the path of blessing through daily actions.
daily: “See, I set before you today a blessing and a curse” (11:26). The word “today” reminds us that the choice is made anew every day.
Service of G-d is tied to the place He will choose — later, Jerusalem and the Temple. Today worshippers all over the world face Jerusalem in their prayers.
Even a miracle does not prove a prophet right if he calls us to turn away from the Torah (13:2–4). Loyalty to the Torah matters more than impressive wonders.
“You are children of the L-rd your G-d” (14:1). From this follows both respect for one's own body and the laws of kashrut, which set apart a Jew's table.
Kosher mammals have split hooves and chew the cud; fish have fins and scales (14:4–10). Kashrut begins with these simple signs.
“Open your hand to your brother, to the poor” (15:8). Tzedakah is not only charity, but the duty to help a person get back on their feet.

“You shall rejoice in your festival — you, and your son, and your daughter, and the Levite, and the stranger, and the orphan, and the widow” (16:14). Festive joy is incomplete if someone has been forgotten.

parashot.summary: The parashah opens with the mitzvah to appoint judges and officers of order in every town and to judge fairly, taking no bribes. Moshe speaks of the supreme court whose rulings must be followed, and of the laws of the king, the kohanim, the Levites and the prophets. Next come the laws of the cities of refuge, of witnesses and of waging war, including the prohibition on cutting down fruit trees. The parashah ends with the ceremony for a murdered person found whose killer is unknown.
parashot.theme: Justice is the foundation of society, and it must be pursued by honest means.
daily: “Justice, justice shall you pursue” (16:20). The commentators explain the repetition this way: both the goal and the means must be just.
“Do not turn aside from what they tell you” (17:11) — the foundation of the authority of the Sages and of the Oral Torah. We study the Torah together with its traditional interpretation.
The king must write a Torah scroll for himself and read it all his life (17:18–19). The higher a person's position, the more humility they need.
“Be wholehearted with the L-rd your G-d” (18:13). Rashi explains: do not try to divine the future; trust G-d with a simple heart.
A charge is established only by the words of two witnesses (19:15). The Torah demands caution before condemning another person.
Before battle, those who had built a house, planted a vineyard or become engaged were sent home, as was the one who was afraid (20:5–8). The Torah remembers a person's feelings even in war.
“Do not destroy the trees” (20:19) — the source of the prohibition on needless destruction, bal tashchit. Caring for the world is also a mitzvah.

parashot.summary: This parashah contains more mitzvot than any other in the Torah: by the count of the Sefer HaChinuch, seventy-four. They concern family and marriage, returning lost items, treatment of animals, home safety, honest trade and care for the worker and the poor. Here too are the laws of tzitzit, divorce and levirate marriage. The parashah ends with the mitzvah to remember what Amalek did.
parashot.theme: Holiness shows itself in everyday life: at home, at work, in trade, and in the treatment of the weak.
daily: The Torah protects the rights of the firstborn, even if the father loves another wife more (21:15–17). Personal feelings must not violate justice.
Having found a lost item, “you cannot hide yourself” (22:3). Returning lost property is an active mitzvah, not mere politeness.
When you build a house, put a railing on the roof (22:8). We are responsible for the safety of those who come to us. This parashah also has the mitzvah of tzitzit on the corners of garments (22:12).
“Do not abhor an Egyptian, for you were a stranger in his land” (23:8). Memory of one's own past teaches gratitude and compassion.
“Whatever comes from your lips, you shall keep” (23:24). Promises and vows are taken very seriously in Judaism, so it is worth being careful with words.
A newlywed is released from the army for a year to bring joy to his wife (24:5). The Torah values family happiness as an important goal.
Pay a worker on the same day (24:15) and keep honest measures and scales (25:13–16). Honesty in business is part of serving G-d.

parashot.summary: The parashah opens with the mitzvah of bringing the first fruits, the bikkurim, to the Temple with a thanksgiving declaration telling the history of the people from the patriarchs to the Exodus from Egypt. Moshe commands that the words of the Torah be written on large stones and that the blessings and curses be proclaimed on Mounts Gerizim and Eival. Then follows a detailed warning about the consequences of abandoning the mitzvot. At the end Moshe reminds them of the miracles of the forty years in the desert.
parashot.theme: Gratitude and memory of the past turn ordinary life into service of G-d.
daily: When bringing the first fruits, a person told the story of the people: “An Aramean sought to destroy my father…” (26:5). These words entered the Pesach Haggadah.
The Rambam rules that a ger also brings the first fruits and says “our fathers,” for Avraham is the father of all who come under the wings of the Shechinah.
The people and G-d “choose” one another (26:17–18). The covenant is a two-sided relationship, not a one-sided demand.
The words of the Torah had to be written on stones “very clearly” (27:8). The Sages understood this as a translation into many languages: the Torah is open to every nation.
Blessings are promised to one who listens to the voice of the Almighty (28:1–14). Blessing is not only prosperity, but also peace and confidence.
The warning explains troubles by saying that G-d was served “without joy” (28:47). Joy in doing mitzvot is not decoration but essence.
“Until this day the L-rd has not given you a heart to understand” (29:3). Understanding comes gradually, with years of study and life according to the Torah.

parashot.summary: Moshe gathers the whole people — from the elders to the woodcutters and water drawers, including the gerim — to enter into the covenant with the Almighty. The covenant is made also with those “who are not here today,” that is, with future generations. Moshe speaks of returning to G-d, teshuvah, and of how the Torah is not in heaven and not beyond the sea, but very close. The parashah ends with a call to choose life; it is read before Rosh Hashanah.
parashot.theme: The Torah is close to everyone, and the way back to G-d is always open.
daily: “You stand today, all of you” (29:9). Everyone takes part in the covenant regardless of status, and the ger is named in this list explicitly.
The covenant was made also with those “who are not here today” (29:14). The Sages teach that at Sinai the souls of future gerim were present as well.
Each person answers for their own choice: one cannot believe it possible to turn away from the covenant in secret and remain apart (29:17–19).
“The hidden things belong to the L-rd, but the revealed things belong to us and our children” (29:28). We are not required to know everything, but we are required to do what is revealed to us.
Chapter 30 speaks of teshuvah: the people will return to G-d, and G-d will return the people. It is a good theme for reflection before Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur.
“It is not in heaven… nor is it beyond the sea” (30:12–13). The Torah was given to people, and it can be understood and kept here, on earth.
“Choose life” (30:19). This is the main decision a person makes again and again, especially at the start of a new year.

parashot.summary: On the last day of his life, at the age of 120, Moshe hands the leadership over to Yehoshua and encourages the people: “Be strong and courageous.” He writes down the Torah and entrusts it to the kohanim and the elders. Moshe commands that once every seven years, on the festival of Sukkot, the whole people be gathered to hear the Torah read. The Almighty warns that in the future He may “hide His face,” and commands that a song of witness be written.
parashot.theme: The Torah is passed from generation to generation, and each person becomes its bearer.
daily: On the last day of his life Moshe himself goes out to the people (31:1). A leader goes to the people; he does not wait for them to come to him.
“Be strong and courageous” (31:6). Resolve is needed not only in battle, but in any new beginning, including the path to giyur.
Moshe publicly transfers authority to Yehoshua (31:7–8). A good transition of generations is prepared in advance and with respect.
Once every seven years the whole people — men, women, children and strangers — gathered to hear the Torah (31:12). This is the mitzvah of hakhel.
“I will hide My face” (31:17–18). Even when G-d's presence is not felt, the connection is not broken.
“Write this song for yourselves” (31:19) — the source of the mitzvah for every Jew to write a Torah scroll or take part in writing one.
The Torah scroll was placed next to the Ark of the Covenant (31:26). The Torah written then is the same text that is read in the synagogue today.

parashot.summary: Almost the whole parashah is Moshe's poetic song, in which heaven and earth are called as witnesses. The song tells of G-d's care for the people, of how the people forget Him in plenty, of punishment and of future redemption. In the Torah scroll this song is written in a special way, in two columns. At the end the Almighty tells Moshe to ascend Mount Nebo, to see the Land of Israel from afar and to die there.
parashot.theme: The history of the people is a history of relationship with G-d, in which distance is always followed by return.
daily: “Give ear, O heavens… hear, O earth” (32:1). Heaven and earth are the eternal witnesses of the covenant, because they remain when generations pass away.
“The Rock — perfect is His work” (32:4). These words are recited at funerals, accepting the judgment of the Almighty even in grief.
“Ask your father, and he will tell you; your elders, and they will say to you” (32:7). The Jewish tradition lives through questions to elders and teachers.
As an eagle hovers over its chicks (32:11), so does G-d care for the people. The commentators see in this an image of tender, careful protection.
“Yeshurun grew fat and kicked” (32:15). Plenty tests a person no less than need.
The song ends with the promise that G-d will stand up for His people (32:36–43). Even after long estrangement, hope remains.
Moshe sees the Land but does not enter it (32:52). Sometimes our task is to prepare the path along which others will go.

parashot.summary: The last parashah of the Torah is read not on an ordinary Shabbat but on the festival of Simchat Torah, right after which the reading begins again with the parashah of Bereshit. Before his death, Moshe blesses each of the tribes of Israel. Then he ascends Mount Nebo, sees the whole Land of Israel and dies; the Almighty buries him, and no one knows his burial place. The Torah concludes with the words that there never again arose a prophet like Moshe.
parashot.theme: The Torah is the heritage of the entire people, and its study never ends.
daily: The Torah ends with a blessing (33:1). Moshe's last words to the people are not a reproach but love.
“Moshe commanded us the Torah, the heritage of the congregation of Yaakov” (33:4). Tradition bids us teach this verse to a child as soon as he begins to speak.
Each tribe receives its own blessing. Every person in the nation has their own path and their own contribution.
“Happy are you, Israel! Who is like you, a people saved by the L-rd?” (33:29). The joy of belonging to the people is the theme of the festival of Simchat Torah.
No one knows where Moshe is buried (34:6). The Sages see in this a lesson: we honor the teaching of Moshe, not his grave.
“There never again arose a prophet in Israel like Moshe” (34:10). This is one of the principles of faith according to the Rambam.
On Simchat Torah, when the reading is finished, Bereshit begins right away. Torah study is a circle without end — a good time to start a new cycle yourself.
